t.6.90.1: Having heard those words spoken by Lakṣmaṇa, Rāghava loosed terrible arrows at Rāvaṇa at the head of the army.
t.6.90.2: But Daśagrīva, standing in his chariot, struck Rāma with exceedingly dreadful arrows like thunderbolts, as a rain-cloud pours down torrents of rain.
t.6.90.3: With arrows adorned with gold, resembling blazing fire, Rāma, fully composed, pierced the ten-necked Daśagrīva in battle.
t.6.90.4: The gods, gandharvas and dānavas declared, "The fight between Rāma, who stands upon the ground, and the rākṣasa, who is mounted on a chariot, is not an equal one."
t.6.90.5: Then appeared the chariot, its body brightly adorned with gold and decked with hundreds of tinkling bells, shining like the newly risen sun, its pole fashioned of beryl.
t.6.90.6: It was yoked with excellent horses, bay in color, bright as the sun, wearing golden crests and white plumes, and adorned with nets of gold.
t.6.90.7: The splendid and excellent chariot of the king of the gods, its flagstaff a golden bamboo, descended from heaven and approached Kākutstha.
t.6.90.9: O Kākutstha, this chariot has been given to you by Sahasrākṣa for your victory, O mighty one; it is splendid and a destroyer of enemies.
t.6.90.8: Then Mātali, the charioteer of the thousand-eyed Indra, standing in the chariot with goad in hand, joined his palms in reverence and spoke these words to Rāma.
t.6.90.11: Mount this chariot, O hero, and with me as your charioteer, O Rāma, slay the rākṣasa Rāvaṇa, as great Indra slew the Dānavas.
t.6.90.10: Here is Indra's great bow, and armor resembling fire, and sharp arrows radiant as the sun, and a spotless spear.
t.6.90.12: Thus addressed, Rāma circumambulated that chariot and saluted it; then he mounted it, illuminating the worlds with his splendour.
t.6.90.13: That wondrous, hair-raising duel of chariot against chariot took place between mighty-armed Rāma and the rākṣasa Rāvaṇa.
t.6.90.14: Rāghava, supreme knower of weapons, struck down the Gāndharva missile of the king of the Rākṣasas with a Gāndharva missile, and the divine missile with a divine one.
t.6.90.15: Then the lord of the rākṣasas, the night-roamer, filled with supreme fury, once again discharged the supreme and terrible rākṣasa weapon.
t.6.90.16: Those arrows adorned with gold, released from Rāvaṇa's bow, turned into highly venomous serpents and rushed toward Kākutstha.
t.6.90.17: With blazing faces, spewing blazing fire from their mouths, those terrifying ones, their jaws gaping wide, rushed straight at Rāma.
t.6.90.18: By those serpents of deadly venom, whose touch was like that of Vāsuki and whose coils blazed, all the cardinal directions were overspread and the intermediate directions were completely enveloped.
t.6.90.19: Seeing those serpents swooping down upon him in battle, Rāma manifested the dreadful Gāruḍa missile, the weapon of Garuḍa, which brings terror.
t.6.90.20: Released from Rāghava's bow, those golden-shafted arrows, blazing like fire, turned into golden Suparṇas, the enemies of serpents, and flew about in every direction.
t.6.90.21: Those arrows of Rāma, able to assume any form at will, took the shape of Suparṇas and struck down all those exceedingly swift arrows that had the form of serpents.
t.6.90.22: When his missile was repelled, Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, enraged, then rained down upon Rāma terrible showers of arrows.
t.6.90.23: Then, having tormented Rāma, tireless in his deeds, with a thousand arrows, he pierced Mātali in return with a flood of arrows.
t.6.90.24: Having struck down the golden banner from the chariot onto the chariot's floor, Rāvaṇa assailed the horses of Indra with a net of arrows.
t.6.90.25: Seeing Rāma afflicted then, the Devas and Gandharvas, the Dānavas together with the Cāraṇas, the Siddhas and the supreme sages were dejected.
t.6.90.26: The lords of the monkeys, together with Vibhīṣaṇa, became distressed on seeing the moon that was Rāma seized by the Rāhu that was Rāvaṇa.
t.6.90.27: Budha, bringing misfortune to the people, stood having overrun Rohiṇī, the constellation presided over by Prajāpati and the beloved of the moon.
t.6.90.28: Then the ocean, its waves rolling amid smoke as though it were ablaze, rose up in fury as if touching the sun.
t.6.90.29: The sun appeared steel-hued and exceedingly harsh, its rays dimmed, its disc marked with the form of a headless trunk, and joined with a comet.
t.6.90.30: And Aṅgāraka stood in the sky, having assailed Viśākhā, the constellation of the Kosalas, plainly presided over by Indra and Agni.
t.6.90.31: Ten-faced, twenty-armed, his bow grasped firmly, Daśagrīva appeared like the mountain Maināka.
t.6.90.32: But Rāma, being driven back by the rākṣasa Daśagrīva, was unable to fit his arrows to the bow at the forefront of the battle.
t.6.90.33: Enraged, he knitted his brows, his eyes somewhat reddened, and he fell into a towering fury, as though burning everything up with his gaze.
